verse.text: Moreover by them is thy servant warned: and in keeping of them there is great reward.
verse.summary: David has just spent ten verses praising God's law as more to be desired than gold, sweeter than honey — and then, almost as an afterthought, he adds the practical payoff: by them is thy servant warned. God's Word doesn't just inspire you, it warns you, like a friend who tells you the truth before the fall instead of comforting you after it. And David doesn't stop at warning — he adds great reward in keeping them. Not in merely hearing them, not in admiring them from a distance, but in keeping them — actually doing what the Word says. The warning saves you from the ditch. The keeping is where the reward lives.

sermon.title: Little by Little, Not All at Once
sermon.excerpt: God never promised Israel an instant Canaan — He promised a mighty hand, a God among them, and a deliverance that would come by little and little.

bibleStudy.title: The Man Who Wouldn't Let Go

verses.text: And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day... And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh. And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me... And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.

He took his brother by the heel in the womb, and by his strength he had power with God: Yea, he had power over the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication unto him: he found him in Bethel, and there he spake with us;
And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint.

bibleStudy.excerpt: A man grabs hold of God in the dark and refuses to turn loose till sunrise — and walks away limping, renamed, and blessed. That's not a strange Bible story. That's your instruction manual for prayer.
body: Picture the scene before you judge the man in it. Jacob has just sent his wives, his children, his flocks, and everything he owns across the river ahead of him, because his brother Esau is coming tomorrow with four hundred men and twenty years of unsettled business. Jacob is alone, in the dark, on the wrong side of the water, with nothing left to negotiate with and nobody left to hide behind. And that is exactly when a man shows up and starts wrestling him.

Nobody wrestles you when you're comfortable. Notice that. God didn't pick a banquet to meet Jacob. He picked the one night Jacob had nothing left to lose and nowhere left to run. If you've ever wondered why your most desperate season turned into your most defining encounter with God, Genesis 32 just answered you.

They go at it all night — no commentary, no explanation, just two figures grappling in the dark until the sky starts to lighten. And here's where the text gets almost comedic if you slow down and actually read it: the "man" wants out. "Let me go, for the day breaketh." The One with all the power in the universe is asking Jacob for permission to leave. And Jacob, dislocated hip and all, says no.

"I will not let thee go, except thou bless me." Read that again. That is not a threat. That is not Jacob overpowering God — three verses later we're told plainly God let him prevail, which means the whole match was a gift wrapped in resistance. That is a desperate man finally doing with God what he had spent his entire life doing with everybody else: holding on and not letting go until he got what he came for.

And that's the part Hosea won't let you skip over centuries later. Hosea 12 looks back at this exact night and tells you two things Genesis doesn't say outright: he had power with God, yes — but he also wept, and made supplication. This wasn't a strongman move. It was a breakdown that turned into a breakthrough. Jacob didn't out-muscle heaven. He out-lasted it, on his knees, in tears, refusing to let go of the only thing in the universe that could actually fix his life.

Now, who is this man wrestling anyway? Hosea calls him "the angel." Genesis calls him God, face to face. Scripture is comfortable holding both without flinching, and so should you — because the point was never a theology quiz on angelology. The point is this: the same man who spent his whole life grabbing — grabbing his brother's heel in the womb, grabbing a birthright with a bowl of soup, grabbing a blessing with a disguise — finally grabbed the right thing. All that grip, all that scheming energy, finally pointed at God instead of at Esau.

And the blessing didn't come free. God touched his hip and it came out of joint, and Jacob walked with a limp for the rest of his life. I need you to sit with that, because we've built an entire culture of faith around the idea that real encounters with God leave you comfortable. They don't. They leave you marked. Nobody walks out of an actual wrestling match with heaven the exact same way they walked in — and if you have never limped away from a season with God, you might want to check whether you actually wrestled, or just watched from the riverbank.

Then comes the new name — and this is the whole sermon in one verse if you let it be. Jacob means heel-grabber, schemer, the guy who gets ahead by leverage and manipulation. Israel means "he struggles with God," or as the angel puts it, "you have power with God and with men, and have prevailed." God didn't rename him Comfortable. God didn't rename him Finally-At-Peace. God renamed him after the very struggle he'd just been through, because the struggle wasn't the obstacle to his identity — the struggle was the forge of it.

So here's my real question for you today, and don't let me preach past it: what have you let go of too soon? One night of prayer and you tapped out. One week of believing and you called it unanswered. We want microwave blessings and drive-through altars, and then we wonder why Jesus had to say it plainly in Luke 18 — men ought always to pray, and not to faint — like He already knew we'd quit right before the daybreak that was about to turn into our breakthrough.

Jacob didn't get his new name by letting go at midnight when it got hard, or at 4am when his hip gave out. He got it by holding on till the sun came up. So hold what you're holding — that prayer, that promise, that person, that healing you keep almost giving up on. Don't let go until He blesses you. Wrestle until daybreak if you have to. Walk away limping if you must. But walk away renamed. In Jesus' name, amen.

lines: Father, thank You for warning me through Your Word before I ever had to learn the hard way — I receive every warning in it today as love, not restriction!
I declare that I am not just hearing Your Word today, I am keeping it — because the reward You promised is not for those who admire the Word, but for those who do it!
Your Word is more to be desired than gold, sweeter than honey, and I choose it today over every cheaper thing competing for my attention!
I declare that every warning I have ignored, every correction I have resisted, I receive now — because the God who warns me is the same God who rewards me!
I will not treat Your Word as information I already know — I will let it search me, warn me, and lead me into the great reward that comes only through keeping it!
Father, make my love for Your Word greater today than my love for being comfortable, because comfort never warned anyone of anything!
So today I lay down the casual way I have sometimes read Your Word, and I pick up reverence for a Book that is still warning and still rewarding right now!
If you've been hearing warnings in your spirit and brushing past them — hear this: the warning was never the hard part of God's love, it was the proof of it.
Save this. Speak it over your obedience today. Moreover by them is thy servant warned, and in keeping of them there is great reward. In Jesus' name, amen!
